source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: how the Pavlovian system sculpts goal-directed choices by pruning decision trees
finding: Founding idea: when people mentally search a tree of choices, they stop evaluating a branch as soon as they meet a large loss. The authors call this a Pavlovian reflex because a negative outcome triggers it.
numbers: Cost saving: 3 binary choices give 8 sequences; cutting at one early large loss removes about half the tree (Fig 1).
limits: Illustrative tree only; in real tasks future values are unknown, so the pruned branch may hide the best path.
agent_relevance: A bad first step is a cheap, automatic cut signal, but it is a bias. Any prune in our agent must be logged and overridable by a check.
quote: they curtailed any further evaluation of a sequence as soon as they encountered a large loss

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: how the Pavlovian system sculpts goal-directed choices by pruning decision trees
finding: Task design: six states, two keys (U, I), deterministic transitions, each move gives a fixed gain or loss. Subjects planned 2-8 moves ahead from a random start. Three groups differed ONLY in the size of the large loss, so the cost of pruning differed by group.
numbers: Large loss -140, -100 or -70 points (large reward +140). Group sizes about 15, 16, 15 (specific-pruning counts 14/15, 12/16, 14/15 subjects). On half of trials the whole sequence had to be entered before any move.
limits: Healthy volunteers screened for pathology; one lab; small groups.
agent_relevance: The design is a template for testing prune rules in an agent: make pruning free in one condition and costly in another, then see if it persists.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: how the Pavlovian system sculpts goal-directed choices by pruning decision trees
finding: Pruning persisted when counterproductive. In the -140 group an equally good path always avoided the loss, so pruning cost nothing. In the -100 and -70 groups pruning cost money, yet specific pruning did not differ between groups.
numbers: Separate-group model had worse iBIC than shared prior. Income lost to pruning grew from group -140 to -100 to -70 (Fig 6C).
limits: Some behaviour differed across groups (more avoidance in -140); the model explained this by reward size, not by smart adaptation.
agent_relevance: Insensitivity to cost is the danger: a loss-triggered prune fires even when the answer lies behind the loss.
quote: pruning was reflexively evoked in response to punishments and relatively insensitive to the ultimate outcomes

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: how the Pavlovian system sculpts goal-directed choices by pruning decision trees
finding: Depth matters. People took the optimal path through a large loss when it came early in a small tree, but failed to when the same subtree sat deeper in a larger tree.
numbers: Depth 4 or 5: optimal sequence chosen more often if the loss was in the first half than the second half (t-tests significant); no difference at depth 6+ (few trials).
limits: Few deep trials, low power at depth 6+.
agent_relevance: Prune pressure rises with search size. Tree rules should bite harder where the tree is big and the budget is tight.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: how the Pavlovian system sculpts goal-directed choices by pruning decision trees
finding: Model ladder. Full look-ahead already predicted choices well, so subjects did plan. One discount parameter helped; splitting it into general and specific (after-large-loss) pruning helped much more; all beat a model-free SARSA habit model.
numbers: Full look-ahead predicted 77% of choices (predictive probability 0.71). Discount model beat the SARSA habit model by an iBIC improvement of 314. Best model (Pruning and Learned) predicted 91% of choices.
limits: Group-level fixed-effects iBIC can overstate evidence across individuals.
agent_relevance: Pruning is a probabilistic stop (a continue-probability), not a hard cut. Code can use a stop probability per branch.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: how the Pavlovian system sculpts goal-directed choices by pruning decision trees
finding: Pruning is not just loss aversion. Models that let each subject weigh losses more heavily did not remove the need for pruning, and adding loss aversion to the best model gave no gain.
numbers: Subjects weighted the largest losses about 1.4 times as much as equal rewards (Fig 5C). Pruning plus loss beat discount plus loss.
limits: The authors say loss aversion may itself be a Pavlovian reaction, so the two may not be fully separable.
agent_relevance: Do not treat prune-after-loss as a mere risk preference. It changes which futures are considered at all.
quote: decisive evidence for specific Pavlovian pruning of decision trees above and beyond any contribution of loss aversion

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: how the Pavlovian system sculpts goal-directed choices by pruning decision trees
finding: A second Pavlovian pull: states that paid out before attract choice even when no moves remain to collect. This Learned Pavlovian term was needed to fit the data.
numbers: From state 6 with 2+ moves left, subjects went to state 1 (small -20 loss, big reward behind) about 90% of the time. With one move left that was wrong, yet about 40% still went there.
limits: Effect rests on one state transition; small sample.
agent_relevance: Two biases to watch: cutting after a loss, and being drawn to previously rewarded options regardless of remaining budget.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: how the Pavlovian system sculpts goal-directed choices by pruning decision trees
finding: Individual differences: stronger specific pruning went with higher sub-clinical depression (BDI, range 0-15). It was specific (not seen for general pruning) and held after controlling age, sex, verbal IQ, working memory and NEO personality. Predicted link with neuroticism was not found.
numbers: BDI correlated positively with specific pruning; negative link with reward sensitivity did not survive multiple-comparison correction. Exact p-values were stripped from the HTML text I read.
limits: Very mild symptoms in healthy sample; later not replicated (see Lally 2017 and Faulkner 2022 lines).
agent_relevance: Little direct use, but shows pruning is trait-like and varies by person, so a prune threshold should be tuned, not fixed.

source: Dayan and Huys (2008) Serotonin, inhibition, and negative mood
finding: Founding formal model: trains of thought are a Markov decision process; serotonin stochastically ends a train of thought when it reaches an aversive state. Continuation probability falls exponentially with negative value at rate alpha_5HT; positive values always continue.
numbers: Simulation: 400 internal states per sign block, 100 terminal states per sign, 8 outgoing links per state, gamma 0.9, learning rate 0.05, 20,000 learning trains, alpha_5HT = 20 for the main run.
limits: Toy model; no human data in this paper.
agent_relevance: A clean spec for a loss-triggered prune: P(continue) = 1 if V>=0, falling exponentially with alpha when V<0. Can be coded directly.
quote: The more disastrous the potential sequelae of state s, the more negative V, and so the less likely the chain was to be continued.

source: Dayan and Huys (2008) Serotonin, inhibition, and negative mood
finding: Pruning biases learning. With strong inhibition aversive outcomes are visited less, so their badness is under-estimated (optimism) while average reward during learning rises. The bias sits mainly in negatively valued states.
numbers: Fig 3: with alpha_5HT = 0 estimates match true values; with alpha_5HT = 20 negative values are poorly estimated and visit rate falls with outcome badness.
limits: Simulation only.
agent_relevance: If the agent learns from pruned search traces it will think bad branches are less bad than they are. Log pruned branches so their value is not silently assumed.
quote: Learning with greater inhibition leads to a more optimistic set of values

source: Dayan and Huys (2008) Serotonin, inhibition, and negative mood
finding: Lowering inhibition after learning (a model of tryptophan depletion) gives a more negative average outcome and large negative prediction errors, because branches that used to be cut are now visited.
numbers: Alpha_5HT reduced after learning at 20; average affective outcome becomes more negative (figure-level; exact values not extracted).
limits: A prediction from simulation, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Removing a prune rule that the learned values were trained under creates a mismatch; change both together.

source: Lally et al. (2017) The neural basis of aversive Pavlovian guidance during planning
finding: Replication in an fMRI sample: people were much worse at choosing the best sequence when it ran through a large loss.
numbers: N=37. Correct 78% (SD 18) when the optimal path had no large loss (ONLL) vs 37% (SD 18) when it did (OLL). Difference 41%, t(36)=12.51, d=2.06. By depth 3/4/5: 34%, 40%, 49% gap (d=1.36, 1.86, 1.70). Trial type x depth F(2,72)=5.58.
limits: Large loss was -70 pence here; healthy volunteers; free-plan trials.
agent_relevance: A large benchmark effect for any bad-first-step test of a model: expect about a 40 point drop that grows with depth.

source: Lally et al. (2017) The neural basis of aversive Pavlovian guidance during planning
finding: Model replication: the pruning model beat the discount model decisively; loss sensitivity added a smaller gain.
numbers: iBIC Lookahead 3052, Discount 2549, Pruning 2472, Pruning+Loss 2466. Improvement discount to pruning 77.5. Variance explained 41.7, 52.5, 54.4, 55.3%. gamma_G greater than gamma_S, t(36)=5.12, d=0.84.
limits: Pruning vs Pruning+Loss gap is only 5.8 iBIC.
agent_relevance: Pruning does not reduce to loss weighting in model comparison.

source: Lally et al. (2017) The neural basis of aversive Pavlovian guidance during planning
finding: Neural basis: a trial-by-trial pruning inclination (KL divergence between discount-model and pruning-model trajectory distributions) tracked subgenual cingulate cortex activity, more at higher depth. This was separate from planning (cerebellum, DLPFC, striatum) and value (ventral striatum, mOFC) networks.
numbers: SGC peak MNI (-6, 29, -2), t(36)=3.87, p_SVC=0.004; depth interaction (-6, 35, -5), t(36)=3.47, p_SVC=0.009. Display threshold p<0.005 uncorrected; small-volume corrected in an a-priori ROI.
limits: N=37; correlational fMRI; ROI-corrected only.
agent_relevance: Supports pruning as its own process, not value computation. A separate prune module in the schema is plausible.

source: Lally et al. (2017) The neural basis of aversive Pavlovian guidance during planning
finding: Partial FAILURE to replicate the depression link: no psychometric variable correlated with the model's pruning estimate. Only state anxiety related to the behavioural ONLL minus OLL gap.
numbers: State anxiety vs gap: t(37)=2.12, p=0.042. No link between depression/trait anxiety and gamma_G minus gamma_S.
limits: Authors note a low range of depression scores; N=37.
agent_relevance: The behavioural effect replicates; the individual-difference story is unstable.
quote: we did not replicate our previous finding that this statistic was correlated with subclinical depression scores

source: Faulkner et al. (2022) A comparison of pruning during multi-step planning in depressed and healthy individuals
finding: Clinical test, unmedicated depressed vs healthy people on the same task. Pruning is robust in both. No group difference and no link to symptom severity.
numbers: N=61 (30 depressed, mean BDI 25.4; 31 healthy, mean BDI 3.0). gamma_S 0.630 vs 0.617, t(59)=0.32, p=0.75, BF10=0.27. Within depressed: BDI vs gamma_S r=0.068, p=0.75; BDI vs gamma_G r=-0.083. Money won did not differ, p=0.73, BF10=0.27.
limits: Recruited from a therapy service; some Bayes factors inconclusive (BF10 0.44 to 0.72); sub-groups untested.
agent_relevance: Failed replication of the depression hypothesis but a third-sample replication of the core effect. Safe to treat pruning as a general human tendency.
quote: Participants robustly pruned branches of decision trees that began with large losses, regardless of the potential utility of those branches.

source: Faulkner et al. (2022) A comparison of pruning during multi-step planning in depressed and healthy individuals
finding: Model details in this sample: the Pruning model with four reward-sensitivity (rho) parameters won. A Pavlovian-attraction term did NOT help here, unlike 2012. Loss aversion did not explain pruning; the large gain was about 3 times as appetitive as the large loss was aversive.
numbers: Healthy rho(-140) -2.60, rho(+140) 7.25; depressed -2.38 and 7.34. gamma_G about 0.12-0.14 in both groups.
limits: Different sample and task version (-140 points); model selection varies across studies.
agent_relevance: Component claims (attraction to rewarded states) are less stable than the core claim (prune after a large loss).

source: Huys et al. (2015) Interplay of approximate planning strategies
finding: Control for confounds: pruning survives a model that also includes hierarchical fragmentation of the plan and memoization of past solutions. Every subject discounted outcomes after large losses more steeply than other distant outcomes.
numbers: N=37 analysed (41 recruited, one excluded; WTAR IQ mean 111). 1-gamma_S < 1-gamma_G for 37/37 subjects, in a model capturing 78% of variance. Continuation after non-large-loss outcomes indistinguishable from 1.
limits: Same task family: depth 3-5 (8/16/32 sequences), 9 s planning, plans entered blind.
agent_relevance: Pruning is not an artefact of plan chunking.
quote: pruning remained a powerful effect even when controlling for fragmentation and reuse as much as possible.

source: Huys et al. (2015) Interplay of approximate planning strategies
finding: People also cut trees by splitting deep plans into subgoals, solving greedily, and reusing remembered sub-plans. Pruning acts inside these fragments.
numbers: Subjects searched to the end of each fragment but stopped at large losses within fragments. Mean fragment length did not significantly correlate with verbal IQ. Subgoal choice leaned on the salient large reward.
limits: Subgoal choice was idiosyncratic across people.
agent_relevance: Pair loss-pruning with explicit subgoal splitting and a plan cache, but expect greedy errors at the joins.

source: Guitart-Masip et al. (2012) Go and no-go learning in reward and punishment: interactions between affect and effect
finding: Companion Pavlovian-bias paradigm: reward cues push toward action (go), punishment cues push toward inaction (no-go). Punishment prediction supports passive choices.
numbers: N=47. Action x valence F(1,45)=40.15, p<0.001; action main effect F(1,45)=14.51. Go better under reward and no-go better under punishment: t(46)=4.85 and 5.08, both p<0.001. Winning model adds a Pavlovian term (fraction of state value added to go).
limits: Motor go/no-go, not mental search; shows the general valence-to-inhibition bias only.
agent_relevance: Pruning is one instance of a wider coupling of negative valence to inhibition. Justifies a bias test: does a negative cue make the model less willing to continue?
quote: Instrumental learning is contingent on overcoming inherent and plastic Pavlovian biases

source: Cools, Nakamura, Daw (2011) Serotonin and dopamine: unifying affective, activational, and decision functions
finding: Theory frame for the serotonin link: dopamine and serotonin as opponent systems, serotonin tied to behavioural inhibition and aversive prediction, with repeated caveats that evidence for a causal chain is incomplete.
numbers: Review; no effect size. Notes that acute tryptophan depletion raises risky choice in primates and rats.
limits: Authors stress many caveats and interpretation difficulties.
agent_relevance: The serotonin mechanism for pruning is still a hypothesis; no direct human pruning drug test is cited here.

source: Keramati, Dezfouli, Piray (2011) Speed/accuracy trade-off between the habitual and the goal-directed processes
finding: Computational neighbour: a normative model that arbitrates habit versus goal-directed search by trading search time for accuracy. It names pruning (incomplete consideration of the tree) as a source of goal-directed uncertainty but models it only as added noise.
numbers: Fitted to outcome-sensitivity and reaction-time patterns; no pruning-specific numbers.
limits: Pruning not explicitly modelled, so it does not test Huys.
agent_relevance: Rational-resource view: some pruning is optimal when search is costly. Pavlovian pruning is the version that fires regardless of cost.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: deliberate problem solving with large language models
finding: LLM use of pruning: Tree of Thoughts has the model propose thoughts, score them, and keep only the best b (breadth) or drop sub-trees below a threshold. This is value-based pruning, not loss-triggered Pavlovian pruning.
numbers: GPT-4 Game of 24 (100 tasks): input-output 7.3%, chain of thought 4.0%, CoT self-consistency k=100 9.0%, best of 100 CoT 49%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%.
limits: Does not test a Huys-style loss bias; GPT-4 is the scorer and is fallible.
agent_relevance: Pruning by a scored evaluation with several branches kept beats plain sampling at matched nodes. Keep b>1.
quote: in Game of 24, while GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting only solved 4% of tasks, our method achieved a success rate of 74%.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: deliberate problem solving with large language models
finding: Cost of bad pruning in an LLM: in mini crosswords the evaluator's pruning cut solvable branches (it called valid rare words impossible). Without pruning it solved 4 of 20 games, 3 of which the pruned version could not.
numbers: Crosswords letter/word/game success: ToT 78/60/20%; ToT without prune 65.4/41.5/5%; without backtracking 54.6/20/5%; with oracle best state 82.4/67.5/35%.
limits: 20 games, DFS limited to 100 steps; no human comparison.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of Huys: a cut driven by a looks-bad signal loses some solutions behind it. Keep pruned states revisitable.
quote: Given the state evaluation as a pruning heuristic is imperfect, we also explore ablating the pruning, and find the performance generally worse

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: how the Pavlovian system sculpts goal-directed choices by pruning decision trees
finding: Boundary condition: a fixed reflexive prune can still look sensible. Because general and specific pruning interact with depth, the same model predicts subjects go through a large loss near the root but avoid it deeper in the tree, without any clever adaptive rule.
numbers: In the -70 group subjects chose the optimal path with an early large loss over an equally good path with a late one (Fig 4F). Both pruning rates must satisfy a depth-dependent inequality; fitted group means fell in the allowed region (Fig 4G).
limits: Authors say this is not a necessary consequence of the model and would not hold for all reward sequences.
agent_relevance: A prune rule that is fixed and cheap can produce depth-dependent behaviour; test it at several depths before judging it.
